title: The Orchard Beehives
sum: Eleven-year-old Tess counts bee visits on her family's apple orchard, finds out why the creek trees grow lumpy apples, and writes a letter asking for bees of their own.

cast.d: an eleven-year-old girl who counts everything and writes it all down
cast.look: an eleven-year-old girl with a long brown braid, an orange cap, and a green notebook in her back pocket

cast.d: Tess's seven-year-old brother, loud, funny and a little scared of bees at first
cast.look: a seven-year-old boy with messy blond hair, a striped T-shirt and green rubber boots

cast.d: Tess and Otto's mom, who runs the family apple orchard
cast.look: a woman in her forties with a sunburned nose, a checked work shirt and a clipboard

cast.d: the beekeeper who brings her hives to the orchard every spring
cast.look: a woman in her fifties with short gray hair, a white bee suit with the veil pushed back, and a smoker in one hand

p: Rosa's truck rumbled up the orchard lane at ten o'clock at night, and Tess knelt on her bed to watch it through the window. In the headlights, the apple trees looked white and puffy, as if it had snowed on them in the middle of May. Thousands of blossoms had opened that week, and every one of them needed a visit from a bee.

“Why does she always come in the dark?” Otto asked from the other bed. Mom was standing in the doorway, pulling a sweater over her head. “At night the whole bee family is at home,” she said, “so Rosa can close the entrances without leaving anybody outside.”

Tess was out of bed before Mom had finished talking. She followed her down the lane in pajamas and rubber boots and watched Rosa lift twelve white wooden boxes off the truck, one after another. Rosa arranged them in a long row beside the barn, with every little entrance facing the sunrise. When Tess put her ear against the nearest box, it hummed low and steady, like the refrigerator at home. “About twenty thousand bees in that one,” Rosa said.

By nine the next morning the whole orchard was buzzing, as bees poured out of the entrances and zipped away into the white trees. Otto stood on the porch steps and refused to come any closer. “They can see me,” he said.

At the kitchen table, Mom frowned at her clipboard, because last year the apples had been small and lumpy, and there hadn't been many of them. “Each blossom only stays open for a few days,” she said. “I wish I knew whether the bees were visiting all of them.”

“Somebody could count them,” Tess said. Mom laughed into her coffee. “Who has time to count bees?” Tess did, because it was Saturday, and she had a notebook, a watch and the magnifying lens she had gotten for her birthday.

She chose a branch near the barn and tied a red ribbon around it. The blossoms grew in bunches of five, and this branch had eight bunches, so she drew forty little circles in her notebook. For fifteen minutes she would watch, adding a dot to a blossom's circle every time a bee landed on it.

For the first minute nothing happened, and then a bee dropped onto the top bunch. Tess leaned in with her lens, and suddenly the bee looked as big as her thumb, fuzzy all over and dusted with yellow. Two fat yellow lumps sat on its back legs, like saddlebags on a tiny horse.

The bee pushed its head deep into the blossom to drink. When it climbed out, its fuzzy belly brushed the sticky green tips in the middle of the flower, and a few yellow grains stayed behind. Tess made her first dot, and then another bee arrived, and another, until her pencil could hardly keep up.

Rosa came over with her smoker and bent down to look. “That yellow dust is pollen,” she said, “and a blossom needs some on those sticky tips, or it can't turn into an apple.” Tess looked up from her lens. “So no bee, no apple?” “No bee, no apple,” said Rosa.

Otto had crept as far as the next tree when a bee landed on his sleeve. He froze like a statue, with both arms sticking straight out and his eyes as round as buttons. “Tess,” he whispered, “Tess, Tess, Tess!”
“She's only resting,” Rosa said, “so stand still and she'll leave.” The bee cleaned its feelers, walked down to his cuff and flew away, and Otto let out an enormous breath. “She liked me,” he said.

When the watch finally beeped, Tess went through her circles one bunch at a time. Some blossoms had two or three dots, and a few had none at all. Thirty of the forty had at least one visit. At the top of the page she wrote 30 out of 40 and drew a box around it.

Mom read the number over her shoulder and copied it onto her clipboard. That evening the bees flew home in a steady stream, and the white boxes hummed louder than ever. Otto waved to them from the porch and called, “Goodnight, twenty thousand bees!” “Times twelve,” said Tess.

art.s: At night beside a red barn, a beekeeper in a white bee suit unloads white wooden hives from a pickup truck while an eleven-year-old girl in pajamas and rubber boots holds a flashlight under apple trees in full white blossom.

q.q: Rosa said, “No bee, no apple.” Why does an apple blossom need a bee?
c: The bee brings pollen to the sticky tips.
The bee's buzzing helps the petals open.
The bee eats the petals so an apple can grow.
The bee keeps other bugs off the blossom.
q.e: Pollen sticks to the bee's fuzzy body and rubs off on the sticky tips of the next blossom. Without pollen, there is no apple.

q.q: Draw Otto the moment the bee landed on his sleeve. Give him a speech bubble.
look: Otto frozen like a statue, arms stuck out
a speech bubble with what he whispered
q.e: Otto's frozen face tells the whole story. Nice work!

q.q: What percent of the blossoms on Tess's branch got a bee visit? Tell how you figured it out.
q.a: 75 percent. Thirty out of forty is the same as three out of four, and three out of four is 75 out of 100.
q.e: 30/40 = 3/4 = 75/100. Three out of every four blossoms got a bee.

p: On Monday it rained, and on Tuesday it rained even harder, until brown puddles filled the spaces between the rows. The thermometer on the barn said 9 degrees, and the twelve white hives beside it were almost silent. A few bees crawled out onto their little doorsteps, looked at the sky and went straight back inside.

“They're having a pajama day,” Otto said. Rosa was checking the hives in her raincoat. “When it's colder than about thirteen degrees, most of them won't fly,” she said, “and they absolutely hate rain.”

Tess watched from the barn door and chewed her pencil. The blossoms only lasted a few days, and two of those days were going down the drain. She was also worrying about the creek block, the twenty trees at the bottom of the hill. Last year those trees had grown the smallest, lumpiest apples on the farm.

On Saturday, thirty of the forty blossoms on her barn branch had been visited in fifteen minutes. She wanted the same count by the creek, but a sunny Saturday and a rainy Tuesday were completely different. If the numbers came out different, how would she know whether the place or the weather was the reason?

Then she had it. She would count both places on the same morning, at the same minute, on two branches with the same number of blossoms. That way, the only difference would be the place. There was just one problem: nobody can stand at the top and the bottom of a hill at once.

“I can do dots,” Otto said at supper, when she described the plan. Wednesday came up sunny but cool, and Tess tied a ribbon around a creek branch with eight bunches of five blossoms, forty in all. Otto got an identical barn branch, plus a pencil and a clipboard of his own, and he held them as if he'd been promoted.

At exactly nine o'clock the old dinner bell clanged on the porch, and both watches started together. The air under the willows felt damp and chilly, and Tess's key-ring thermometer said 11 degrees. Up by the barn, as Otto reported later, the big thermometer said 15.

The bees were slow to arrive at the creek. One landed, drank and buzzed away, and then nothing happened for a long time. A big bumblebee bumbled through and visited four blossoms in a row, and Tess counted every one. When her watch beeped, she had dots on twelve blossoms out of forty.

Otto came running down the hill with his clipboard over his head like a trophy. He had counted with his tongue sticking out the whole time, and his dots were neat: twenty-eight blossoms out of forty. “I win,” he said. “It's not a race,” Tess said, but she stared at the two numbers side by side for a long time.
Mom came down with her coffee and checked the thermometer. “Cold air is heavy,” she said. “At night it slides downhill and settles in the low spots, like water in a bowl, and the creek is our bowl.”

Rosa had followed her down, and she pointed uphill at the long row of hives beside the barn. “Bees work close to home when there's plenty of bloom,” she said. “Why fly all the way down here when there's lunch next door?” Otto had an answer immediately: “Then move two hives to the creek!”

Rosa shook her head. “Move a hive across the orchard, and the bees fly straight back to the old spot,” she said. “They'd be standing around in the grass by the barn, looking for their front door.” Otto laughed so hard he had to sit down.

Rosa had a better idea. That night, in the dark again, she brought two more hives from her own bee yard, twenty kilometers away. Bees moved that far can't find their way back, so they learn the new place instead. She set the boxes at the edge of the creek block. “Don't stand in front of the entrances,” she said, “because that's their runway.”

In the morning Otto made a cardboard sign that said BEE RUNWAY — WALK BEHIND THE BOXES. Underneath, he drew a bee in pilot goggles. When the first bee zoomed out of the new hive and right over the sign, Otto saluted. “Cleared for takeoff,” he said.

art.s: On a cool sunny morning in the low corner of an apple orchard, two white beehives stand under willow trees by a creek, with a small boy's cardboard sign on a post and bees flying out of the hive entrances.

q.q: What percent of the creek blossoms got a bee visit?
q.e: 12 out of 40 is the same as 3 out of 10, which is 30 out of 100. That's 30%.

q.q: Why did Tess and Otto count at the same time, on branches with the same number of blossoms?
q.a: So the only thing that was different was the place. Then if the numbers came out different, Tess would know it was the place, not the weather or the time.
q.e: Change one thing and keep the rest the same. Then you know what made the difference.

q.q: Rosa called the space in front of the hive entrances the bees' “runway.” Draw the creek hives and their runway, with Otto's sign.
look: bees taking off from the hive entrances like little planes
an empty space in front of the entrances
q.e: Runways are for planes, but one word from Rosa turned the bees into pilots!

p: At the end of June, Otto came running up from the creek with the front of his T-shirt held out like a basket. It was full of little green apples, each one about the size of a marble. “The trees are breaking!” he shouted. “They're throwing all their apples on the ground!”

Mom was sitting on the shed step sharpening her pruning shears, and she hardly looked up. “That's the June drop,” she said. “Every summer the trees let some of them go, like somebody packing light for a long trip.” Otto frowned, because he had never packed light for anything in his life.

Tess picked one of the little apples out of his shirt and turned it over in her fingers. It was hard and slightly fuzzy, and one side was flatter than the other. Why would a tree drop this apple and keep the others? She held it out to Mom and asked her to cut it open.

Mom unfolded her pocketknife and sliced the apple across the middle, right through its belly. Inside was a pale green star with five points, and when Tess looked through her lens, she saw that each point was a tiny pocket. “Seeds grow in there,” Mom said, “up to two in each pocket.”

Tess counted two seeds, white and small like grains of rice, sitting together in one pocket, while the other four pockets were completely empty. Then Mom reached up, picked an apple that was still hanging on the tree beside the shed and cut that one open too. This time Tess counted eight seeds, spread all around the star.

“Two in the one that fell,” Tess said, “and eight in the one that stayed.” Mom wiped the knife on her jeans. “Each seed needs its own grain of pollen,” she said, “and the seeds help the apple grow, so a side with no seeds stays small.” Tess remembered last year's creek apples, squashed on one side like a pillow somebody had sat on.

Even after the June drop, the trees still carried too many apples. If every one of them stayed, they would all grow up small, and a heavy branch could even crack. So every summer the family pinched off the extras by hand, and Mom called this job thinning. This afternoon the creek block was theirs to thin.

Mom's rule was simple: one apple in each bunch, the biggest one, and pinch off the rest. Tess started on a low branch and counted everything first, because she always counted first. The branch had eight bunches with twenty-four little apples altogether, and some bunches had two apples while others had four.

She kept the biggest apple in each bunch and pinched off the others, which dropped into the bucket, plink, plink, plink. Otto stared at her with his mouth open. “You're throwing away apples!” “I'm making room,” Tess said, “so these eight can get all the food.”

Otto didn't look convinced. He rescued a few pinched apples from the bucket and lined them up on the ladder step, just in case. Then he tried to roll one into the bucket from three steps away. He missed eleven times in a row, and the twelfth one bounced off Tess's boot.

By late afternoon their arms ached from reaching. Tess cut one last apple, from the tree beside the two hives Rosa had placed by the creek in the spring. Inside it were nine seeds. She drew the star in her notebook and wrote a big 9 next to it, with a circle around the number.

At supper Otto set a tiny green apple beside every plate and called them appetizers. Mom took a bite of hers, and her whole face puckered up like a drawstring bag. “Packing light,” she said, and she dropped it into the compost bucket.

art.s: Beside a garden shed under apple trees in early summer, a mother cuts a marble-sized green apple in half with a pocketknife while a girl studies the five-pointed seed star through a magnifying lens and a small boy holds out a T-shirt full of tiny green apples.

q.q: What fraction of the little apples on Tess's branch did she keep?
q.e: She kept 8 of the 24 apples. 8/24 is the same as 1/3.

q.q: Mom said the trees were “like somebody packing light for a long trip.” What did she mean?
q.a: She meant the trees were dropping some of their little apples, so they had fewer to carry and feed. That way the apples that stay can grow big.
q.e: Packing light means taking only what you can carry. The tree lets go of the extras.

q.q: Draw the two apples Mom cut open: the one that fell and the one from the tree. Show the seeds in each star.
look: a five-pointed star inside each apple
2 seeds in the apple that fell
8 seeds in the apple from the tree
q.e: More seeds, better apple. Now you can see why the tree kept the second one!

p: By the middle of July, the orchard was quiet. Rosa had taken all fourteen hives away after the blossoms fell, off to a clover field where her bees could make honey. The apple trees were thick with leaves, the little apples had grown to the size of golf balls, and nothing in the rows hummed anymore.

Then one afternoon, walking along the fence with Otto, Tess heard it. The ditch beside the fence was full of white clover and purple vetch, and it was buzzing. Fat, striped bumblebees climbed in and out of the flowers. Tiny black bees she had never noticed before were working the clover heads, two and three at a time.

She looked back at the orchard, where the grass between the rows was mowed short without a single flower in it. The apple blossoms had been gone for six weeks. When Otto asked where the bees could eat now, Tess pointed at the ditch. “It's the only restaurant in town,” she said.

She had been thinking about the creek trees all summer, because they stood in a cold, low corner, far from where Rosa usually put her hives. If the farm kept two hives of its own down there, the creek blossoms would never have to wait for bees. And if flowers grew along the fence after the apples finished, the wild bees would have food all summer and still be around next May.

At lunch she told Mom the whole idea at once. Mom ate an entire sandwich before she said anything. “Hives cost money, seed costs money, and bees need somebody to look after them,” she said. Then she tapped the table. “Write me a letter, and give me reasons, not wishes.”

The first letter took Tess about five minutes. “Dear Mom, bees are amazing and I love them, so can we please have our own? I promise to take care of them forever. Love, Tess.” Otto thought it was the best letter ever written, but Mom read it and handed it back. “That's a lovely wish,” she said.

Tess spread her notebook across the kitchen table, with its dots from blossom week and its seed stars from June. She found the morning when she and Otto had counted at the same time. By the barn, 28 blossoms out of 40 had been visited, but by the creek it was only 12 out of 40. She turned both results into percents and wrote them in big numbers.

Next she needed to know how big a flower strip would be, so she and Otto carried Mom's long tape measure out to the fence. The tape only reached thirty meters, so they measured twice and found that the strip was 60 meters long and 2 meters wide. At the farm store, the bag of buckwheat seed promised flowers in about six weeks.

Her second letter took all afternoon. “Dear Mom, I think we should keep two hives of our own by the creek and plant buckwheat along the fence. On the same morning, 70 percent of the barn blossoms had a bee visit, but only 30 percent of the creek blossoms did. The creek apples that fell in June had almost no seeds inside. After the blossoms are gone, the ditch is the only food the bees have left, and buckwheat flowers in six weeks. I will do all the watering. Love, Tess.”

Mom read the letter at the kitchen table, and then she read it again with a pen in her hand. She tapped the 30 percent twice. “This part is hard to argue with,” she said. “The strip, yes, and we'll plant it tomorrow.”
When Tess asked about the hives, Mom folded the letter into her shirt pocket. “Ask me again at harvest,” she said, “and if the creek trees do better this year, we'll talk.”

The next morning they raked the strip along the fence until it was a long brown rectangle of soft dirt. Tess walked the length of it, throwing seed in wide swings, while Otto threw his in handfuls over his head, like confetti at a wedding. By lunch the bag was empty, and there were buckwheat seeds in Otto's hair.

art.s: Along a wooden orchard fence on a summer morning, a girl scatters buckwheat seed over a long strip of raked brown dirt while her little brother throws seeds over his head like confetti, with green apple trees behind them.

q.q: Mom called Tess's first letter “a lovely wish.” What was missing from it, and what did Tess add to the second one?
q.a: The first letter only told how Tess felt. The second one had evidence, like the 70 percent and 30 percent bee counts and the seeds in the fallen apples.
q.e: A wish tells what you want. Evidence tells why it's a good idea.

q.q: Why did Tess want a flower strip along the fence?
c: The apple blossoms were gone, and bees needed other food.
The flowers would stop the June drop.
Bees need tall stems to build their nests on.
The strip would give the apple trees more shade.
q.e: Bees need flowers all summer, not just in blossom week. In July the ditch was the only food left.

q.q: Draw the flower strip as a rectangle. Label how long and how wide it is, then write its area inside.
look: 60 m on the long side and 2 m on the short side
q.e: 60 × 2 = 120 square meters. That's room for a lot of buckwheat!

p: On the Saturday before school started, the creek apples were finally ready. They were an early variety, always the first on the farm to be picked, and this year the branches bent under their weight. Tess cupped one in her hand, lifted and twisted, and it came off with a snap. When she bit into it, juice ran down her chin.

Along the fence, the buckwheat strip was in full bloom, knee-high and white. It buzzed from one end to the other with bumblebees and tiny black bees, all of them too busy to notice Otto. He sniffed a flower and made a face. “It smells like socks,” he said, and he was not wrong.

Back in July, Tess had written Mom a letter asking for two beehives of their own, and Mom had told her to ask again at harvest. Today was harvest. Last year's notebook lay open on the tailgate of the truck. On the creek page, Mom had written that the trees averaged two and a half crates each. Tess's job was to count the crates from the first five trees in the row.

They picked all morning, with Mom on the ladder and Tess on the low branches. Otto ran the empty crates out and chalked each tree's number on the full ones. The first tree filled 4 crates, and the second filled 5, which made Otto perform a victory dance on the tailgate. The third tree had lost a branch in a July storm and filled only 3, and after that came 5 again, and then 3.

Near the bottom of the last crate, Otto discovered an apple with one flat side and held it up like a precious fossil. “Why is this one lumpy?” Tess held up five fingers and touched them one at a time: “Crabapple, bee, blossom, seed, apple.”

Otto waited. “That's not a sentence,” he said, so Tess tried again. “Pollen from a crabapple blossom rides on a bee to an apple blossom,” she said. “Each seed needs its own grain of pollen, and the seeds help the apple grow, so a side with no seeds stays flat.” To prove it, Mom cut the lumpy apple in half with her pocketknife, and on the flat side, the pockets of the star were empty.

Tess added up the crates in her notebook, five trees and twenty crates altogether, and then she did the division and underlined the answer twice. She set her notebook on the tailgate right next to Mom's old one, so that the two numbers sat side by side.

Mom studied the two numbers for a long time before she spoke. “Maybe it was just a better spring,” she said. “It rained for two days in blossom week, and the creek was four degrees colder than the barn,” said Tess. “The only new thing down there was Rosa's two hives.”

Just then a truck came up the lane, in daylight for once, and Rosa climbed out to buy a crate of apples for her kitchen. Mom showed her the two notebooks, and Rosa gave a long, low whistle. “That letter of yours had a stinger in it,” she told Tess.

Mom laughed. “It certainly did,” she said. “Two hives by the creek next spring, with Rosa finding us the bees and you doing the looking after.” Tess's ears went hot, and she hugged the nearest crate, which was a mistake, because it was full of apples and very hard.

Rosa reached into the back of her truck and lifted out two empty white hive boxes. “Paint them over the winter,” she said, “but only in light colors, because a dark box soaks up the sunshine and gets too hot.” That evening Otto painted a bee in pilot goggles on each one, and Tess added CREEK HIVE 1 and CREEK HIVE 2 in tall blue letters.
The boxes sat drying on the porch, still empty, and Otto patted their lids before he went inside for supper. “Goodnight, zero bees,” he said. “See you in May.”

art.s: On a sunny late-summer afternoon at the edge of an apple orchard, crates of red apples are stacked beside a pickup truck, a strip of white buckwheat flowers blooms along the fence, and a beekeeper hands two empty white hive boxes to a girl and her little brother.

q.q: Rosa said Tess's letter “had a stinger in it.” What did she mean?
c: It made a point that was hard to say no to.
It said something mean about the orchard.
It had a drawing of a bee at the bottom.
It came in a yellow-and-black envelope.
q.e: A stinger is sharp. Tess's letter had a sharp point: real evidence that was hard to argue with.

q.q: What was the average number of crates for the five creek trees this year? Show how you worked it out.
q.a: 4 crates per tree. The five trees filled 4 + 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 20 crates, and 20 crates shared evenly by 5 trees is 4 each.
q.e: 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Last year it was 2.5, so that's 1.5 more crates per tree!

q.q: Draw Tess's five-finger chain. Show how pollen got from a crabapple blossom to a round apple.
look: a bee carrying pollen from a crabapple blossom
the bee landing on an apple blossom
a round apple with seeds inside
q.e: Crabapple, bee, blossom, seed, apple. You drew the whole chain!

fin.q: Sum up the creek trees' story in two or three sentences. What was wrong, what did the family do, and how did it turn out?
fin.a: The creek trees stood in a cold, low spot far from the hives, so few bees visited and the apples came out small and lumpy. Rosa put two hives by the creek, and Tess wrote Mom a letter asking for hives of their own. At harvest the creek trees filled more crates, and Mom said yes.
fin.e: A good summary keeps only the big parts: the problem, what they tried and how it ended.

fin.q: Why did the creek trees grow more apples this year than last year?
c: The two creek hives brought more bees to the blossoms.
The buckwheat strip fed the blossoms in the spring.
The spring by the creek was warmer this year.
The June drop took no apples from the creek trees.
fin.e: The buckwheat was planted in July, long after the blossoms. The new thing in blossom week was the two creek hives, and more bees meant more pollen and more seeds.
